doc.title: John Abercrombie interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: His guitars
summary: The Brian Moore, Jim Mapson archtop, and his collection of guitars he keeps playing.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Right. For our guitar viewers, what’s your instrument of choice these days?

Well I brought to the concert tonight I brought two instruments. It’s funny because I was just listening to a couple of recordings coming up and for a long, for many years I played an Ibenez style Les Paul, then I switched to a Roger Sedowski telecaster style instrument,

which is on a lot of those recordings, which is a wonderful instrument. And then I switched more recently to a guitar made by a company called Brian Moore. It’s called Brian Moore Custom Guitars. It’s not custom made for me, but it’s like a Les Paul with a switch for the guitar guys, a five way switch that you could move it and split the pick-ups and make it sound like single coil pick-ups if you want. It’s got a beefy, fat sound. It’s got a nice bridge pick-up and also under the bridge it has a piezo pick-up, which is sort of a fake acoustic pick-up for those that don’t know. It’s like a little crystals. Actually I don’t know how this one works but they’re under each string. And if you listen with your eyes closed from a distance of like several thousand yards it almost sounds like it’s an acoustic instrument. So I used that kind of blended in with the magnetic pick-ups, with the regular guitar pick-ups, and I find it’s an interesting, it creates an interesting sound. It still sounds like the guitar but gives it a little bit of shine it doesn’t have normally. And I also brought a handmade guitar by a wonderful maker in California named Jim Mapson, which is like a little, very thin bodied archtop with one, just a pick-up in the neck. And I’ll probably play that on a couple of tunes because it is a pretty open guitar so in a certain situation it may feedback a little but it’s a wonderful instrument. So those are the two I’m playing mostly right now. I have a roomful of guitars.

We tend to collect. Yeah I don’t know how it happens. I had an old Les Paul, I’ve got my Ibanez, I’ve got a wonderful old 175, a used 175 from the 50s, which I never bring on the road but it’s probably the best guitar I have. I have two handmade guitars by a maker named Rick McCurdy in New York that are wonderful, a big archtop and then a small body guitar, also lovely. And I have played them, they’ve all been on the road, they’ve all been on a record date, I mean they’ve all had some use but you can’t use them all the time, which is a shame, I wish I could just have about ten hands, I could just like go around and play them all at once every day, just to keep everybody happy out there. Sometimes I think I should do that, just open up the case and say okay, now I’m going to play you for five minutes, and then at least we’ve communicated today.
Good karma. Well I think it’s important. If an instrument sits too long it can die. I had a beautiful old guitar kind of die on me years ago, an acoustic instrument. And it’ll happen.
